article.title: Second Conditional
article.description: Structure: If + past simple, ... would + base verb. Used for hypothetical or unlikely present/future situations: 'If I won the lottery, I would travel the world.' Common mistake: using 'would' in the if-clause too — 'If I would win the lottery' is incorrect; the if-clause always uses past simple.
article.content: Structure: If + past simple, ... would + base verb. Used for hypothetical or unlikely present/future situations: 'If I won the lottery, I would travel the world.' generated.caption:
Ever dream about winning the lottery? 🤩 That's where the **Second Conditional** shines!

We use 'If + past simple, ... would + base verb' for hypothetical or unlikely situations. Just remember: the 'if' clause always takes past simple, never 'would'.

Example: "If I won the lottery, I would travel the world."

slides.headlineRest: — Master Unlikely Scenarios (And Avoid This Mistake!)
slides.body: The Second Conditional is a crucial grammar structure used to talk about hypothetical or unlikely situations in the present or future. Its structure is 'If + past simple, ... would + base verb.' For instance, 'If I won the lottery, I would travel the world.' A common error is using 'would' in the 'if'-clause, like 'If I would win the lottery,' which is incorrect. Remember, the 'if'-clause always takes the past simple, never 'would.'
